patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral foot numbness and weakness for 14 months with recent right wrist drop
patient.history_present_illness: Thomas Gu is a 49-year-old sales director presenting to neurology after developing progressive bilateral foot numbness over 14 months followed by recent onset right wrist drop noted upon awakening 3 weeks ago. He initially attributed his foot symptoms to long hours standing during business travel and tight footwear. His primary care physician obtained EMG 3 months ago which reportedly showed mild sensory neuropathy and attributed it to borderline prediabetes (HbA1c 5.9%). However, the acute onset of right wrist drop was alarming, and the patient was referred urgently. He reports left hand numbness as well (ring and little finger distribution). He has been evaluated for occupational exposures: he works in pharmaceutical sales and denies any chemical exposures. He has noted a 6 kg unintentional weight loss over the past year which he initially attributed to stress and dietary changes. He has also noted intermittent abdominal fullness and early satiety for 6 months. He is a non-smoker and drinks socially but not heavily. He has never used intravenous drugs. He has a maternal grandmother who had 'Charcot foot' from diabetes, and he was therefore not concerned initially. His right wrist drop is now impacting his ability to drive and write, prompting this urgent referral.

specialized_test.impression: ABNORMAL NCS/EMG — mononeuritis multiplex pattern. Axonal injury involving multiple separate nerves: right radial (severe amplitude reduction with acute denervation on EMG), left ulnar (moderate amplitude reduction, subacute changes), bilateral peroneal (moderate-to-severe amplitude reduction, chronic reinnervation). Amplitude-predominant loss without conduction block. Pattern localizes to multiple individual peripheral nerves in separate anatomic territories, following a stepwise asymmetric course. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: VASCULITIC NEUROPATHY CONFIRMED. Epineurial necrotizing vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis of medium-sized vessel wall. Transmural eosinophilic and neutrophilic infiltrate. Axonal degeneration in multiple fascicles. Eosinophilic infiltrate in vessel wall raises EGPA.

report.summary: CT CHEST: Bilateral ground-glass opacities in both lower lobes consistent with eosinophilic lung disease (eosinophilic pneumonia pattern). Small bilateral pleural effusions. No nodules, no cavitation. CT ABDOMEN/PELVIS: Circumferential wall thickening of distal ileum and cecum — eosinophilic gastroenteritis pattern. Mild mesenteric lymphadenopathy. No mass lesion. GI wall thickening explains iron deficiency anemia (GI blood loss from eosinophilic gastroenteritis), thrombocytosis (reactive), and hypoalbuminemia.
report.clinical_significance: Bilateral lower lobe eosinophilic pneumonia pattern and eosinophilic gastroenteritis pattern identified. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.interpretation: Abnormal values: BAL Differential — Eosinophils 42% % (H), BAL Macrophages 38% % (H), BAL Neutrophils 18% % (H), BAL Lymphocytes 2% % (H).

report.summary: Echocardiogram: LVEF 60% (normal). Mildly increased pericardial effusion (8 mm, trivial-small). No wall motion abnormalities. No valvular abnormalities. No evidence of eosinophilic endocarditis. Pericardial effusion is likely EGPA-related (cardiac involvement in EGPA 20-50%).
report.clinical_significance: Small pericardial effusion identified. No evidence of constrictive physiology. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Colonoscopy: patchy erythema and mucosal edema from cecum through distal ileum. Biopsies show eosinophilic infiltrate (>50 eosinophils per high-power field) in ileum and cecum — consistent with eosinophilic gastroenteritis. No polyps. No malignancy. No IBD features.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA / Churg-Strauss) with mononeuritis multiplex
critical_actions: Recognize mononeuritis multiplex — do NOT attribute to prediabetes or prior NCS showing mild distal sensory neuropathy
Order ANCA (MPO/PR3) urgently in any patient with mononeuritis multiplex — vasculitic neuropathy
Multi-organ assessment: lung, heart, GI — EGPA is systemic
Nerve biopsy to confirm vasculitis histologically before committing to cyclophosphamide
Echocardiogram — cardiac EGPA can cause fatal myocarditis and restrictive cardiomyopathy
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute wrist drop to pressure palsy without workup — mononeuritis multiplex requires vasculitis exclusion
Do not attribute to prediabetes — HbA1c 5.9% prediabetes does not cause mononeuritis multiplex
Do not delay treatment while awaiting all biopsies in patient with rapidly progressing vasculitic neuropathy
Do not start IVIG — this is vasculitic neuropathy requiring steroids and immunosuppression, not CIDP

differential.key_features: HbA1c 5.9% in prediabetic range does not cause acute wrist drop; length-dependent bilateral symmetric pattern expected; mononeuritis multiplex is not diabetic neuropathy
MPO-ANCA present in both MPA and EGPA; EGPA is distinguished by eosinophilia >1000 cells/uL (at peak), eosinophilic organ involvement (lung, GI), nerve biopsy eosinophilic infiltrate

differential.diagnosis: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNPP)
differential.key_features: HNPP causes painless focal pressure palsies at common compression sites; systemic features absent; ANCA negative; eosinophilia absent; family history negative
MMN causes conduction block without axonal loss; no sensory involvement; anti-GM1 IgM typically positive; no systemic features

key_reasoning_points: MODERATE DIFFICULTY: Prior NCS labeled 'mild diabetic neuropathy' and HbA1c 5.9% prediabetes create strong anchoring bias
KEY ALERT: ACUTE WRIST DROP is never attributable to prediabetes — demands urgent vasculitis workup
EGPA triad: eosinophilic lung disease + peripheral eosinophilia + neuropathy — systemic features point beyond pure neuropathy
Unintentional weight loss + early satiety + GI symptoms + microcytic anemia = systemic disease, not isolated neuropathy
MPO-ANCA is positive in ~40% of EGPA (unlike PR3-ANCA which is rarer) — must be tested
Eosinophilia in peripheral blood + eosinophilic vasculitis on nerve biopsy = EGPA vs MPA (eosinophilia distinguishes EGPA)
Mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) is FDA-approved for relapsing/refractory EGPA — modern alternative to cyclophosphamide
